1:
The title's wilderness is disputed before the psalm begins. Clarke reports that the ancient versions and several Latin fathers read Idumea for Judah, but rules against them: "there is no evidence that David had ever taken refuge in the deserts of Idumea. The Hebrew text is that which should be preferred; and all the MSS. are in its favor." Augustine, working from the reading Clarke rejects, builds his whole exposition on it — "by the name of Idumæa is understood this world", the desert signifying "this life, wherein we suffer so great toils". The thirst carries its promise, since "he that thirsteth in this world, in the world to come shall be satisfied."

Calvin and Henry keep to the Judaean flight and trace it. Calvin lists the hiding-places — Hareth, Ziph, Maon, Engedi, "all in the tribe of Judah" — and calls the psalm not so much prayer as "a variety of pious meditations, which comforted the mind of David under dangers, anxieties, and troubles of a severe description". Henry observes that it will be so "in the world, in the church, but not in heaven; there it is all city, all paradise, and no desert ground", and that "the best and dearest of God's saints and servants may sometimes have their lot cast in a wilderness". Delitzsch adds a liturgical fact nobody else records: this was "the morning Psalm of the ancient church with which the singing of the Psalms was always introduced at the Sunday service".

"Early will I seek thee" is read as waking rather than as haste. Ellicott notes the ancient versions render it "to thee I wake early", and that this "was certainly in the Hebrew, since the verb here used has for its cognate noun the dawn" — "the expectancy which even in inanimate nature seems to await the first streak of morning" shows the connection. Wesley keeps the plain sense, that morning "implies the doing it with diligence and speed". Gill grounds the possession in covenant, not birth — God "was his God in the wilderness of Judea, as in his palace at Jerusalem" — and Spurgeon presses the confidence into a rebuke: "he has no doubts about his possession of his God; and why should other believers have any? The straightforward language of this opening sentence would be far more becoming in Christians than the timorous and doubtful expressions so usual among professors."

What was seen in the sanctuary divides literal from spiritual. Gill offers the ark, "as the Jewish writers generally interpret it", or rather Christ. Clarke keeps it to public ordinances, where God showed power "in the judgments he executed" and glory "in delivering the tempted, succouring the distressed" — whence "public worship should never be neglected". Ellicott alone rearranges the verse, the received English "weakening the sense": read rather "so, in the sanctuary have I had vision of thee in seeing thy might and glory" — since "while he saw with his eyes the outward signs of Divine glory, he had a spiritual vision" of God. Wesley reduces the seeing to enjoying.

On lovingkindness better than life they compete in extravagance. Gill argues from the negative: "life without the love of God is nothing else than death: a man that has no share in the love of God is dead while he lives"; and it "lasts longer than life, and therefore must be better than that". Clarke presses the plural — better than lives, "good beyond countless ages of human existence" — Henry marks how quickly the psalm turns: "faithful prayers may quickly be turned into joyful praises, if it be not our own fault", David being "now in a wilderness" and yet with "his heart much enlarged in blessing God". Clarke explains the lifted hands from the custom by which "pious Jews, in every place of their dispersion... stretched out their hands towards Jerusalem".
5:
The banquet image is handled with different degrees of caution. Ellicott clears away one association in a sentence: this figure, "which repeats itself so frequently in Scripture, need not be connected with the sacrificial feasts." Gill goes the other way and makes the legal connection the point. Fat "was not to be eaten under the legal dispensation, and therefore not to be literally taken"; David understood the typical sense, "or otherwise he would speak contrary to the law of God". Clarke measures the satisfaction against its earthly counterpart: in true worship there is "as complete a sensation of spiritual sufficiency and happiness, so that no desire shall be left unsatisfied, as any man can have who enjoys health of body, and a fullness of all the necessaries... of life." Wesley keeps it conditional, referring it to the fulfilled desire to be in the sanctuary.

On the night watches Ellicott supplies the framework and Clarke the practice. Ellicott corrects the tense to a past, notes the plural beds, and gives the Jewish reckoning of three watches — "the beginning, or head; the middle; and the morning". Gill draws the plural into biography: David lay in many beds, "being obliged to flee from place to place", and it is when "alone, and free from worldly cares and fatigues" that the recollection comes. Clarke turns the verse into a rule of the bedside: "I will lie down in thy fear and love; that I may sleep soundly under thy protection... and when I awake in the night watches, or be awakened by them, I will spend the waking moments in meditation upon thee."

What the sheltering wings are is the tile's real question, and it has two answers that nobody quite chooses between. Henry sets them side by side. The phrase may allude "to the wings of the cherubim stretched out over the ark of the covenant, between which God is said to dwell" — so that the rejoicing is "in thy oracles, and in covenant and communion with thee" — or "to the wings of a fowl, under which the helpless young ones have shelter". He distinguishes two birds within the second image: the eagle's young, which "speaks the divine power", and the common hen's, which "speaks more of divine tenderness". Clarke gives the same alternatives with the same reluctance to decide. If the psalmist does not mean the mercy-seat "over which the cherubs extend their wings", he may have in view "the young of fowls, seeking shelter, protection, and warmth under the wings of their mothers" — and adds what makes the metaphor exact: "when a bird of prey appears, the chickens will, by natural instinct, run under the wings of their mothers." Ellicott only rebalances the clauses — "for thou hast been my helper; and under the shadow" — and Delitzsch marks the turn, the closing strophe now turning "towards these foes", the party from which the psalmist has retreated into the desert.

The last verse is where the Hebrew is pressed hardest, and all three reach the same place by different routes. Clarke renders it "my soul cleaves, or is glued, after thee", finding three things at once: "the diligence of the pursuit, and the nearness of the attainment, but also the fast hold he had got of the mercy of his God." Ellicott says the verb "combines two ideas" — cleaving and following — and offers the English idiom that captures both: "hung upon thee". Gill takes the cleaving as union, "such an one as is between man and wife, who cleave to each other, and are one flesh", and specifies the object negatively before positively — not the world, not what is evil, not the creature, but "the summum bonum".
9:
The turn to the enemies is read as retribution in kind. Spurgeon states the principle twice over: "destroyers shall be destroyed. Those who hunt souls shall be themselves the victims" — "into the pits which they digged for others they shall fall themselves. The slayers shall be slain, and the grave shall cover them." Gill limits what the enemies could actually reach: they sought his life, "for as for his soul, that was immaterial and immortal, and could never be destroyed by man".

Where "the lower parts of the earth" leads divides the literal from the infernal. Clarke gives both: they are "appointed, in the just judgment of God, to destruction; they shall be slain and buried in the earth, and shall be seen no more" — but "some understand the passage as referring to the punishment of hell; which many supposed to be in the center of the earth", and he quotes the Old Psalter's Middle English for that reading, "thai sall entir in till lagher pine of hell". Ellicott keeps it to the underworld.

Verse 10 is where the Hebrew resists the English. Ellicott renders it "more literally, they shall pour him on to the hands of the sword", the suffix being "collective of the enemy", so that the meaning is "they shall be given over to the power of the sword"; and he corrects the animal — not foxes but jackals. Clarke reaches the same rendering by another road, "they shall be poured out by the hand of the sword", and offers two constructions of the second clause: either the bodies are "left unburied, and the jackals shall feed upon their dead bodies", or, the men being "all cut off by utter destruction, their inheritance shall be left for the wild beasts". Gill fixes the fulfilment on Saul and his sons, with antichrist as the type's later term.

Who the rejoicing king is produces three answers and one rejection. Gill dismisses the suggestion that it means Saul, and offers David himself, "anointed by Samuel, and who, upon the death of Saul, was so in fact", rejoicing "not merely at the destruction of his enemies, for he lamented the death of Saul", but in God's goodness; or rather the King Messiah, rejoicing "because of the good of his people". Wesley takes the plainest line — "I who am already anointed king". Clarke holds a Davidic and an exilic possibility open together: David "shall come to the kingdom according to the promise of God", or, if the psalm belongs to the captivity, "the blood royal shall be preserved in and by Zerubbabel till the Messiah come."

What it is to swear by him is the tile's last uncertainty, and Ellicott lays out both sides without forcing a choice. The phrase is explained as meaning "swear allegiance to him as the king", which "suits the context"; on the other hand "the natural way to understand the phrase" is of "the only oath allowed to the Israelite, by the name of Jehovah". On that construction the promise divides the loyal from the false: those "who appeal to Him in all troubles" shall glory, "while the unfaithful and false, not daring to make the solemn appeal, will have their mouth stopped." Clarke supplies the custom behind the first reading — it was usual "to swear by the life of the king" — but thinks the reference here may be to God, swearing by whose name means "binding themselves by his authority, acknowledging his supremacy, and devoting themselves to his glory and service alone". Wesley restricts the swearers to those who do so "in truth, and judgment, and righteousness", that is, "every sincere servant and worshipper of God".
